newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway makes peace with tax-burdened peacekeepers.
newsitem.headline: Norway makes peace with tax-burdened peacekeepers.

text.p: The Norwegian government reached a deal with its peacekeepers in Bosnia and Lebanon on overseas taxation on Thursday, ending a tax revolt that resulted in hundreds of them handing in their resignations.
The national news agency NTB said the association of military officers (BFO) and the finance ministry agreed on a contract under which overseas allowances would not be taxed after all.
In addition, soldiers will receive an additional 2,000 crowns ($280) every six months and a free home trip, NTB said.

"This is a good result we hope will satisfy the soldiers," BFO spokesman Sindre Mork was quoted as saying. "We are proud that so many of the soldiers handed in their resignations, but we hope they will now withdraw them."

The resignations were submitted last weekend by about a thousand of the 1,600 Norwegians -- from privates to generals -- serving in peacekeeping missions for NATO and the United Nations in Bosnia and Lebanon.
Defence Minister Joergen Kosmo, reacting promptly to the mass resignations, on Sunday pledged to strike a deal with the finance ministry within a week so that no soldier would lose any money.

The soldiers, the pride of Norway's acclaimed commitment to international peacekeeping, learned a week ago that the finance ministry had decided to tax, retroactively from January 1, the allowance paid to soldiers working overseas.
The fringe benefit, granted to soldiers to compensate for extra expenses resulting from living abroad, was previously exempt from taxation.

BFO complained that soldiers stood to lose between 30,000 and 55,000 crowns a year each because of the new rule. A sergeant earns an average 300,000 crowns a year and is taxed betwen 30 to 40 percent on the income. ($ = 7.142 Norwegian Crowns)
